source.title: Slices of Brownian Sheet: New Results, and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Let B = {B(s,t)}_{s,t ≥ 0} be a d-dimensional two-parameter Brownian sheet, and for each s > 0 consider the zero set of the slice t ↦ B(s,t), namely {t > 0 : B(s,t) = 0}. When d ∈ {2,3}, does there exist an event of probability one on which, simultaneously for every s > 0, this slice zero set B^{-1}{0} ∩ ({s} × (0,∞)) is a finite set?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 1. Suppose d ∈ {2 , 3}. Is it true that outside a single null set, B−1{0} ∩ ({s} × (0 , ∞)) is a finite set for all s > 0?
Theorem 1.2. If d ∈ {2 , 3}, then the following holds outside a single P-null set: dimH(B−1{0} ∩ ({s} × (0 , ∞))) = 0 for all s > 0.

accepted.question_text: For a d-dimensional two-parameter Brownian sheet B and each s ≥ 0, define Y_d(s) = {(t_1,t_2) ∈ R_+^2 : B(s,t_1) = B(s,t_2)}, the double-point set of the slice at level s. When d ∈ {4,5}, does there exist an event of probability one on which, simultaneously for every s ≥ 0, the Hausdorff dimension of Y_d(s) is equal to 0?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 2. Define, for all s ≥ 0, Yd(s) := {(t1, t2) ∈ R2+ : B(s , t1) = B(s , t2)}. Then is it the case that if d ∈ {4 , 5} then, outside a single null-set, dimH Yd(s) = 0 for all s ≥ 0?
Theorem 5.1 and a codimension argument together imply that with probability one, dimH Dˆd = (3 - d/2)+, and dimH D¯d = 2 ∧ (3 - d/2)+.

accepted.question_text: For a d-dimensional two-parameter Brownian sheet B and each s ≥ 0, let Y_d(s) = {(t_1,t_2) ∈ R_+^2 : B(s,t_1) = B(s,t_2)}. When d ∈ {4,5}, does there exist an event of probability one on which, simultaneously for every s > 0, the set Y_d(s) is finite?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 3. Let d ∈ {4 , 5}. Then is it true that outside a single null set, Yd(s) is a finite set for all s > 0?
Open Problem 1 has the following analogue for double-points.

accepted.question_text: Let B be a d-dimensional two-parameter Brownian sheet, let B^{-1}{0} be its zero set, and consider orthogonal projections of B^{-1}{0} onto lower-dimensional subspaces. Is there a random orthogonal projection for which the projected set has Hausdorff dimension different from 2 - d/2?
accepted.context_brief: Projected dimension of the zero set

evidence.quote: Open Problem 4. Is there a (random) orthogonal projection such that the said projection of B−1{0} has a different Hausdorff dimension than 2 - (d/2)?
Consequently, when d ∈ {2 , 3}, the [Hausdorff] dimension of Zd is equal to 2 - (d/2).

accepted.question_text: Let Ḃ_1, ..., Ḃ_d be independent two-dimensional white noises, let b: R^d → R^d be bounded and Borel measurable, and let σ: R^d → R^d be a strongly elliptic, bounded, C^∞ function. For the nonlinear hyperbolic stochastic PDE system ∂^2 u_i/∂t∂x = b_i(u) + σ_i(u) · B̂ with reasonable boundary conditions, do the results proved earlier in the paper for Brownian-sheet slices continue to hold for the solution u?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 5. Suppose σ : Rd → Rd is a strongly elliptic, bounded, C∞ function. Is it the case that the results of the previous sections apply to the solution of (∂^2u_i/∂t∂x) = b_i(u) + σ_i(u) · B̂ with reasonable boundary conditions?
Consider d independent, two-dimensional white noises, B˙1, . . . , B˙d, together with the following system of d non-interacting stochastic PDEs with additive noise:

accepted.question_text: Consider the linear parabolic SPDE system ∂u_i/∂t (t,x) = ∂^2 u_i/∂x^2 (t,x) + B̂_i(t,x) with reasonable boundary conditions, where the driving noises are independent space-time white noises. Is there an analysis of the time slices t ↦ u(t,·) for different values of t that is analogous to the slice results proved in this paper for the Brownian sheet?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 6. Consider the following system of linear parabolic SPDE: ∂ui/∂t (t , x) = ∂^2u_i/∂x2 (t , x) + B̂_i(t , x), with reasonable boundary conditions. Is there an analysis of the “slices” of u along different values of t that is analogous to the results of the present paper?
Finally, we end with an open-ended question about parabolic SPDEs, about which we know far less at this point.
